subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Rise of Detroit
description: A 60-second lesson on The Rise of Detroit.

hook.text: Detroit wasn't always the Motor City. It became one because of geography and timing.

buildup.text: Michigan had lumber, iron, copper, and Great Lakes shipping—perfect raw materials for building cars.

discovery.text: When Ford, GM, and Chrysler all set up there, suppliers followed. A car ecosystem was born.

twist.text: At its peak, Detroit made 80% of all American cars. One city powered an entire industry.

climax.text: But when foreign competition arrived decades later, that concentration made Detroit very fragile.

punchline.text: The same focus that built Detroit later broke it.

quiz.question: Why did Detroit become the Motor City?
options: It had the most skilled workers

details.summary: Detroit became the world's automotive capital in the early 1900s because of its location near iron, timber, and waterways, combined with a skilled workforce from the carriage and shipbuilding industries.
details.whyItMatters: Detroit's rise as Motor City shaped American industry, labor relations, and urban development for a century, creating millions of jobs and defining middle-class prosperity.
takeaways: Ford, GM, and Chrysler all headquartered in the Detroit area
Proximity to raw materials and waterways gave Detroit an edge
The city's population surged from 285,000 in 1900 to 1.5 million by 1930

faq.question: Why did Detroit decline as an automotive center?
faq.answer: Automation, outsourcing to cheaper regions, competition from Japanese imports, and the 2008 financial crisis devastated Detroit's economy. The city filed for bankruptcy in 2013 but has since begun recovering.

faq.question: Are cars still made in Detroit today?
faq.answer: Yes. The Big Three still operate major facilities in the Detroit area, though production is far more distributed globally. Detroit remains the headquarters for GM, Ford, and Stellantis's North American operations.
